editorial_contributions.text:
\textit{D. G. Larman} and \textit{C. A. Rogers} [Mathematika 19, 1--24 (1972; Zbl 0246.05020)] introduced the concept of \((M,D,\delta)\)-critical configurations in \(\mathbb{R}^n\): \(M\) points, such that among any \(D+1\) of  these points the distance \(\delta\) occurs between two points. This concept is crucial as lower bounds for the chromatic number of the unit distance graph in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are based on finding \((M,D,1)\)-critical configurations in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
with a large \(M/D\) ratio. The paper under review investigates how big \(M\) can be in an \((M,3,1)\)-critical configuration in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and proves an upper bound of \(O(n^{3/2})\). (This result has been improved further to \(O(n^{4/3})\), building on ideas of the paper under review, by \textit{A. Kupavskii} et al. [Comb. Probab. Comput. 28, No. 2, 280--286 (2019; Zbl 1435.52008)].) A number of  results are given about the maximum \(M\) in low dimension. It is shown that \(M\geq 2n+4\) and it is conjectured that \(M=O(n)\). Note that \((M,3,1)\)-critical configurations have been renamed to almost equidistant sets and the paper uses this new terminology. The paper introduces a more general extremal problem: for positive integers \(d\), \(k\), and \(\ell\) with \(\ell\leq k\), what is the maximum size of a point set \(P\) in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) such that among any \(k+1\) points from \(P\), there are at least \(\ell +1\) points that are pairwise at unit distance. (A similar problem studied previously, with orthogonality instead of unit distance, is also discussed.)

title.title: On almost-equidistant sets

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: A set in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is called almost-equidistant if for any three distinct points in the set, some two are at unit distance apart. First, we give a short proof of the result of \textit{K. Bezdek} and \textit{Z. Lángi} [Period. Math. Hung. 39, No. 1--3, 139--144 (1999; Zbl 0965.51006)] claiming that an almost-equidistant set lying on a \((d-1)\)-dimensional sphere of radius \(r\), where \(r<1/\sqrt{2}\), has at most \(2d+2\) points. Second, we prove that an almost-equidistant set \(V\) in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) has \(O(d)\) points in two cases: if the diameter of \(V\) is at most 1 or if \(V\) is a subset of a \(d\)-dimensional ball of radius at most \(1/\sqrt{2}+cd^{-2/3}\), where \(c<1/2\). Also, we present a new proof of the result of \textit{A. Kupavskii}, \textit{N. H. Mustafa} and \textit{K. J. Swanepoel} [``Bounding the size of an almost-equidistant set in Euclidean space'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:1708.01590}]  that an almost-equidistant set in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) has \(O(d^{4/3})\) elements.
\par For Part I see [the author, Linear Algebra Appl. 563, 220--230 (2019; Zbl 1407.52018)].

editorial_contributions.text:
The book is devoted to various geometrical topics as graphs of functions, transformations, curves and surfaces as well as their applications in many other disciplines. It presents elementary methods for analytical modeling and demonstrates the potential for symbolic computational tools to support the development of analytical solutions. The text integrates traditional and non-Euclidean geometries, differential and computational geometry with more recent computer systems in a practical and user-friendly format. The author systematically examines several powerful tools of \texttt{Matlab} including 2D and 3D animation of geometric images with shadows and colors, transformations using matrices, and then studies more complex geometrical modeling problems related to analysis of curves and surfaces. 

The book is written for a large audience of advanced undergraduate and postgraduate students, engineers and computer scientists, instructors of applied mathematics and it is an excellent textbook to be used in lectures as well as for self-study reference. 

Part 1 (four chapters) studies functions and their graphs, curves and surfaces in classical and modern geometries. 

Chapter 1 can be considered as an introduction to \texttt{Matlab} symbolic and numeric calculations, programming, and basic graphing as needed in later chapters. It starts with some discussions on the geometry of (integer, real, complex, and quaternion) numbers and the necessary notation from algebra. In the following, graphs of some elementary, special, and piecewise functions are plotted and investigated using derivatives. In Section 1.3, the author studies piecewise functions of one variable that are defined by several formulae for different values (intervals) of that variable. The next section presents some remarkable curves (graphs) in polar coordinates. This chapter ends with several \texttt{Matlab} functions that implement various interpolation and approximation algorithms. 

Chapter 2 contains methods and the visualization of Euclidean geometry and covers the following topics: vectors and matrices and their use in analytic geometry, rigid motions or isometries, applications of complex numbers and quaternions, geometry of a sphere in space, and polyhedra. 

Chapter 3 is devoted to affine and projective transformations and their description using matrices and homogeneous coordinates. Such transformations provide the reader with the basic mathematical means of picture manipulation. 

In Chapter 4, the author investigates non-Euclidean geometry based on inversive and Möbius transformations. An important role in this study is played by complex numbers in the two-dimensional case, while in the three dimensional space, quaternions are used as a useful instrument to present these transformations. Reflection (inversion) in a sphere (or a circle) is exploited as a tool for proving results in Euclidean and hyperbolic geometry. The upper half-plane endowed with the Poincaré metric is considered. Many curves (lines, transversals, circles, equidistants, horocycles, fifth lines, etc.) are displayed. 

Part 2 (five chapters) studies differential-geometric models of curves and surfaces and approximation/interpolation of curves and surfaces. The methods (matrices and transformations, complex numbers and quaternions, interpolating and approximating) of Part 1 are also applicable to these specific constructions. 

Chapter 5 starts from the basic notion of a regular curve. Then, cycloidal and other remarkable parameterized and implicitly given planar curves are studied. The level sets are useful in solving problems with conditional extrema. The author describes the variational calculus and employs Euler's equations to study elastica. Some basic \texttt{Matlab} capabilities for plotting space curves using various coordinate systems and (parallel and perspective) projections are also presented. Next, curves with shadows on planar, cylindrical or spherical displays are discussed, as well as fractal curves (Peano, Koch, Sierpiński, Menger) defined recursively. 

Chapter 6 is devoted to the differential geometry of curves. It studies tangents and normals at regular points, arc length, singular points, mathematical embroidery (curves appear as envelopes of families of lines or circles), the curvature and the torsion of a curve, evolutes, caustics and parallel curves, and other constructions with curves. Several programs for detecting singular points on curves, deriving characteristics of space curves, plotting a moving Frenet frame field and the osculating circle, and reconstructing a plane curve from its curvature function are developed. 

In Chapter 7, parametric surfaces and regular surfaces are considered. A big number of \texttt{Matlab} commands are used to produce examples of surfaces by various methods. Tangent planes and normal vectors of a surface, the osculating paraboloid, and the Gaussian and mean curvatures are computed and then plotted, conditional extremum problems are solved and geodesics are plotted, surfaces with singularities are studied, and a short program for investigating the differential geometry of a surface are provided. 

Chapter 8 studies three very important and commonly occurring classes of surfaces (algebraic surfaces, surfaces of revolution, and ruled surfaces) and considers several interesting constructions with surfaces: translation, parallel, pedal, and podoid surfaces, tubes, the envelope of a family of surfaces, etc. 

Chapter 9 is devoted to the study of approximation and interpolation of curves and surfaces. The author focuses on Bézier curves, spline curves and surfaces, the Hermite interpolation technique to construct piecewise curves and \(\beta\)-spline curves.

u/L	o\alpha\in(0,+\infty)\), then \(2t_0/(L^2/
u)\) converges in distribution to \(l_0^{-1}(\alpha\xi)\), where \(l_0\) is the local time at 0 for a standard Brownian motion starting at 1 and \(\xi\) is independent with a mean 1 exponential distribution. An analogical result is obtained for a sequence of voter models on \(Z\). A parabolic differential equation is described for computing the limiting distribution.

This book is an excellent introduction to a lot of aspects of combinatorial theory, and I enjoyed reading it very much. I can recommend it to anybody who wants to learn about combinatorics. A slight disadvantage for some (English oriented) readers might be the language (German).

 Every chapter begins with a short introduction containing the type of problems or objects that are studied in the chapter. Also the work done in the past and present research on the subjects are listed, sometimes together with some historic facts on the life of the inventors of the problems or theorems.

 Sometimes the proofs in the book are somewhat to rigorous and too little intuitive. In some cases somewhat more detail would not harm (for instance the triangulation of a torus is hard to imagine without knowing this kind of things already (Chapter XIV, Excercise 2.3)).

 The chapters on block designs cover almost 70 pages which is 20\% of the book, and this seems to be a little bit overdone. Nevertheless the book probably is the best introduction into combinatorial theory written in the German language.

 Chapter I starts with a short introduction to set theory. The Dedekind definition of finite set is directly followed by the theorem that a set \(M\) is finite if and only if there is a number \(n\) and a bijection from \(M\) to \(\{1,2,\dots,n\}\). This theorem is far from trivial (using Dedekinds definition), and the proof (which is omitted) depends heavily on the axiom of choice (Auswahlaxiom). Some words should be spent on this. Next Newton's binomial and Pascal's triangle are covered. The principle of inclusion and exclusion is discussed and the Möbius and Euler functions are introduced. The problems of menages and rencontres are treated. Permanents are introduced and van der Waerden's conjecture is discussed briefly.

 Chapter II gives an introduction to graph theory and its terminology. The theorem of Hall (marriage theorem) is covered, generalized and applied. The connection with König's theorem on bipartite graphs and the theorem of Dilworth for partially ordered sets is discussed. The assignment problem is mentioned. Next an introduction to Sperner theory is given (the lemma of Sperner). Menger's theorem is given in two versions. The max-flow min-cut theorem of Ford and Fulkerson is discussed. Finally the theorem of Barranyai is mentioned.

 Chapter III is on Latin squares. The definition of mutually orthogonal Latin squares (MOLS) is given. Orthogonal arrays are introduced. Finite fields are touched upon. It would have been nice if Excercise 3.11 was linked to the chapter on finite projective planes (more specific Theorem 2.1 of Chapter IX). A number of existence results and constructions for MOLS and orthogonal arrays are given (MacNeish theorem, constructions with difference matrices). A proof is given for the fact that for every \(n\) unequal to 2 or 6 there exist 2 MOLS, so Euler's conjecture is proven to be false. As an application of orthogonal arrays the relation with optimal authentication codes is shown.

 Chapter IV concerns Arrow's paradox, which states that if in a group of persons every person has a preference sequence for a set of objects and there is a (complicated) rule to determine a general preference based on the list, where the rule satisfies two conditions: unanimity rule and independency rule for every two objects, then in the group there is a dictator (i.e. the preference of one of the persons always matches the general preference). Basically the result says that one does not have a large amount of freedom in specifying the rule if one has to comply with the two conditions.

 Chapter V is a short one and studies ``fast periodic'' sequences, more specific the Morse-Thue sequence and its properties.

 Chapter VI deals with Ramsey's theorem, which is introduced as a kind of generalization of the pigeon hole principle.

 In Chapter VII the famous theorem of van der Waerden on arithmetic progressions is proven. Furthermore without proofs the connected theorems of Szemerédi, and Schur, Rado and Deuber are discussed. The chapter finishes with a proof of the theorem of Hales and Jewet.

 Chapter VIII is concerned with coding and information theory. Strictly speaking these subjects are not part of combinatorics and it is discutable whether an introduction into combinatorics should deal with these subjects. On the other hand there is a close connection between some parts of coding theory and combinatorics, which might justify a treatise of the field. A reader not interested in coding theory could of course skip this chapter. The first subject in the chapter is direct decodable codes, and the Kraft inequality is proved. Next check codes are dealt with, i.e. the digits of codewords satisfy certain conditions such that some types of errors are detected (neighbour swaps and single errors make up 89\% of all errors, so the systems are designed to cover these types of errors). Some existence results are given for such systems, in case the digit set is an abelian group. Next subject is error correcting codes. The three basic upper bounds are proved (Singleton bound, Sphere packing bound and Plotkin bound). The trivial lower bound (Gilbert-Varshamov) is proved. Perfect codes, MDS-codes and equidistant codes are introduced and some references are given to other combinatorial objects. Algebraic coding theory is discussed. Linear codes over finite fields are introduced. Hamming codes are defined and shown to be perfect. The Griesmer bound is treated and the linear variant of the Gilbert-Varshamov bound is discussed. Cyclic codes are introduced and shown to be the ideals in the polynomial ring \(\text{GF}(q) [x]/(x^n- 1)\). BCH-codes are discussed and the binary Golay code is introduced. Furthermore Reed-Solomon codes are shown to be MDS-codes. Next CRC-checks are explained. The chapter closes with remarks on the difficulty of the (general) decoding problem.

 Chapter IX is on projective planes. The axioms are given and the classical ones (coming from the 3-dimensional vector space over a finite field) are discussed. Here an excercise connecting this classical construction (Beispiel 1.7) to Übung 3.11 of Chapter III would be nice. The connection between orthogonal Latin squares and projective planes is shown. Some non-existence results (Bruck and Ryser) are mentioned but the proof is postponed until Chapter XI (on block designs). Polarities are introduced and studied. The theorem of Singer (existence of a cyclic subgroup of the group of automorphisms of the projective geometry \(\text{PG}(n,q)\), with \(q\) a prime power) is given. This leads in a natural way to difference sets. Next (maximal) arcs and (hyper)ovals are introduced. The connection between arcs and MDS codes is given together with some existence results. Furthermore Baer subplanes and blocking sets are discussed. Some cryptographic applications of projective geometry are given, more specific authentication codes and secret sharing schemes are designed using objects in projective geometry. Finally affine geometries are treated. The extension of affine planes to projective planes should have been discussed more extensively, for instance the stated parallel classes come out of the blue. In three excercises Gauss coefficients are introduced and used to count the number of subspaces satisfying particular conditions.

 Chapter X gives an introduction to the theory of block designs. Starting with the Kirkman schoolgirl problem, some classical cases are discussed. Then, some necessary conditions on the parameters of a block design are proved (including Fisher's inequality). Next some constructions are given using difference sets in groups. Group divisible designs and transversal designs are introduced and the connection with orthogonal arrays is shown. Furthemore some constructions methods for constructing new PBDs from known ones are given. This leads to the theorem that the necessary conditions for the case \(k=3\) and \(\lambda= 1\) are also sufficient. The chapter finishes with some observations on solvable block designs.

 Chapter XI continues with symmetric block designs. Again a number of necessary conditions on the parameters is given. This includes the theorem of Bruck-Ryser-Chowla. A connection with Hadamard matrices is given and some constructions for Hadamard matrices are discussed, among which the famous Paley construction. Also the Kronecker product construction is treated. Some constructions for other symmetric block designs are given, including some multiplier constructions using cyclotomic cosets. The construction of difference sets (Problems 6.12, 6.13 and 6.14 of this chapter) is fun.

 Chapter XII treats partitions. Their generating functions are discussed. The notions of Ferrers diagram and Durfee square are introduced. The strength of using Ferrers diagrams is shown in giving two proofs of the Euclidean pentagonal theorem.

 Chapter XIII deals with Pólya's theorem. The cycle index of a permutation group is defined. The fundamental lemma of Burnside is treated, and some applications are shown. The same holds for Pólya's theorem to finish the chapter.

 Chapter XIV is on some combinatorial aspects of topology. Subjects treated in this chapter include the Königsberger bridge problem on Euclidean cycles in graphs, the polyeder formula of Euler (that can be used to prove the nonexistence of Platonic polyeders other then the tetraeder, the cube, the octaeder, the dodecaeder and the icosaeder), the five color theorem (with a proof), some theorems on Hamiltonian cycles in graphs, the lemma of Sperner on simplicial tilings, Brouwers fix point theorem and finally Helly's theorem on intersections of convex sets.

 Chapter XV gives some theory on games and graphs. The classical NIM-games are discussed. The kernel for games is defined. NIM-sums and Grundy functions are introduced.

 Chapter XVI, the last chapter of the book, is dealing with (integer) sequences. Starting with the Fibonacci sequence it goes across the menage numbers, the rencontre numbers, partition numbers, Catalan numbers, Bell numbers, Stirling numbers (of both kinds), and finally Gauss coefficients. The book ends with an extensive literature list consisting of suggestions for further reading.

 During my reading of the book I found the following (more or less serious) errors and typo's.

 On page 3 the symbol for Durchschnitt (intersection) should be read upside down (a \(\cap\) instead of a \(\cup\)) (4th line from below).

 On page 20 under formula (3.9) it is stated incorrectly that the number \(D_n\) asymptotically equals \(1/e\), however the fraction is asymptotical equal to \(1/e\), as stated correctly in formula (3.10). On page 24 the notation \(f\) and \(F\) is used continuously for the same ``Befreundungssystem''. Furthermore in the proof \(D(d)\) must be \(f(d)\) (or \(F(d)\)). This page really needs a consistency check on notations.

 On page 43 under the picture the flow goes from \(q\) to \(s\) in stead of from \(s\) to \(t\) (to be consistent with the pictures).

 On page 90 in the first picture in the left part \(P\) and \(C\) are interchanged. In the proof on page 90 the 3rd line should be \(M\in\text{perm}(A)^P\) instead of \(M\in\text{perm}(A)\).

 On page 143 in definition 3.4: \(K=B\) or \(B=K\)?

 On page 145 underneath \(*: \theta= (q- 1)/q\) instead of \(\theta= (q- 1)q\).

 On page 262 Gleichung (6.3) must be Gleichung (5.5), though actually the equations (5.5) and (6.3) are the same, but a reference should never be made to a future equality.

 On page 267, 3rd line from under Satz 6.6 should be Korollar 6.6.

editorial_contributions.text:
This book under review gives a systematized and impressive account of the research of the author during the last some fifteen years, written in a well understandable English with some Romanic flavour and featured by a large amount of physical details in this mathematical text, and of pictures showing computing results, often in colours.

The long title already shows what is to be awaited but the content is divided into two main parts: hyperbolic quasi-linear balance laws (you understand: not just conservation laws but equations with the named differential operator and a right hand side: a source term), and weakly nonlinear kinetic equations.

After an introductory chapter there follow: Lifting of a non-resonant scalar balance law (the condition of non-resonance rather often being posed to be able to prove convergence and accuracy results); Lyapunov functional for linear error estimates (here also a convincing example is given that the customary time splitting, for an accretive source term, is not leading to an acceptable error growth like \(O(\sqrt{t})\) but to exponential growth!); Early well balanced derivations for various systems, Viscosity solutions and large-time behavior for non-resonant balance laws; Kinetic scheme with reflections and linear geometric optics; Material variables, strings and infinite domains, whereas the second part contains the chapters: The special case of 2-velocity kinetic models, Elementary solutions and analytical discrete-ordinates for radiative transfer; Aggregation phenomena with kinetic models of chemotaxis dynamics (this being one of the important applications of the theory); Time-stabilization on flat currents with non-degenerate Boltzmann-Poisson models (semiconductor equations are another important application); Klein-Kramers equation and Burgers/Fokker-Planck model of spray; A model for scattering of forward-peaked beams; Linearized BGK model of heat transfer; Balances in two dimensions: kinetic semiconductor equations again; Conclusion: Outlook and shortcomings.

Whereas the first chapter already clarifies that there will be no mathematical definition of the term ``well balanced'' which goes back to \textit{J. M. Greenberg} and \textit{A.-Y. Le Roux} [SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 33, No. 1, 1--16 (1996; Zbl 0876.65064)], and everybody knows what is meant like in the case of the term ``stiff'', Chapters 2 and 3 show the general procedure: the 1D balance equation is written as a \(2\times 2\) homogeneous Temple system, the former source is approximated by a weighted sum of Dirac delta functions (for this approach, convergence is proved in the weak-* topology). For numerical computing, this boils down to an enlarged Godunov scheme (the seminal paper of whom is cited only in Chapter 3 though it well could be subsumed under the title ``well balanced'') in which there is, however, an additional step resulting the values at the jumps (with subsequent solution of Riemann problems). For those latter values, the steady-state equation is solved remembering the Scharfetter-Gummel approach for semiconductor equations, or that of \textit{R. Eymard, J. Fuhrmann} and \textit{K. Gärtner} [Numer. Math. 102, No. 3, 463-495 (2006; Zbl 1116.65101)], for 2D nonlinear parabolic equations. Of course, these additional computations need their attention and computing time and, ideally, lead to small linear equations (like in the numerous physical examples of Part II). An error estimate for the proposed ``non-resonant Godunov scheme'' is given in Chapter 3. Further theoretical results are obtained, e.g., in Chapter 5: Existence, uniqueness, \(L^1\)-stability and large-time behaviour for bounded variation viscosity solutions of balance equations.

In the second part, often there are 2D linear equations for which two approaches are shown: either the differential (or integral) operator is developed in terms of an appropriate function system or the 2D operator is discretized à la \textit{P. L. Roe} and \textit{D. Sidilkofer} [SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 29, No. 6, 1542--1568 (1992; Zbl 0765.65093)]. Then the well balanced method of the first part is applied.

There follow three appendices: Non-conservative products and locally Lipschitzian paths; A tiny step toward hypocoercivity estimates for well-balanced schemes on \(2\times 2\) models; and Preliminary analysis of the errors for Vlasov-BGK.

Every chapters has its own references and often ends with notes reviewing the results reached and discussing their relation to works by other authors.

Interesting is, e.g. a discussion in the Notes at the end of Chapter 15: ``It may be worth insisting on the fact that sometimes, reducing a 2D model into a tricky one-dimensional formulation can constitute an interesting strategy \dots'' -followed by examples. Well, sometimes, but 2D models should reveal more details and insights. The 1D models considered in the book are nonlinear, the 2D equations are mainly linear (and approximated by the optimum positive scheme of Roe and Sidilkover) and usually are less fast convergent than discrete equations stemming from 1D, necessitating perhaps finer discretizations. Even then, there should not be a problem in solving them using Matlab's \(x=A\backslash b\), and if nonlinear, in employing some iteration. Finally, why generalizing to 2D only by looking for appropriate places to put point-Dirac delta functions onto lines of an equidistant grid? Is there no possibility to employ at least Dirac functions concentrated on pieces of lines?

Also, not too much words are lost on the handling of boundary conditions; mostly, specular conditions are assumed but for Boltzmann-Poisson equations (Chapter 11) there is a special paragraph on these matters. What concerns the numerous figures, it seems more a decision of the editing house to give them a measure which forces the reader to use a magnifying glass.

All in all, a book interesting for mathematical researchers in partial differential equations and for physicist, bringing a wealth of fresh ideas and methods much improving the time splitting approach.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: We investigate the relationship between weak asymptotic symmetry ($\mathrm{WAS}$) and asymptotic symmetry ($\mathrm{AS}$) for quasisymmetric maps associated with planar quasilines. To this end, we introduce a formally weaker condition, called equidistant weak asymptotic symmetry ($\mathrm{EWAS}$), and prove that, for quasisymmetric embeddings of $\mathbb{R}$ into $\mathbb{C}$, the three conditions $\mathrm{AS}$, $\mathrm{WAS}$, and $\mathrm{EWAS}$ are equivalent. We then establish that $\mathrm{WAS}$ implies $\mathrm{AS}$ for quasisymmetric homeomorphisms from an arbitrary quasiline onto $\mathbb{R}$. More generally, if $h\colonΓ_1\toΓ_2$ is a quasisymmetric homeomorphism between quasilines and $Γ_1$ is asymptotically conformal, then $\mathrm{WAS}$ implies $\mathrm{AS}$. A formally dual statement holds when $Γ_2$ is asymptotically conformal, provided that $h$ is uniformly continuous. In the compact setting of bounded quasicircles, these results yield an answer to the $\mathrm{WAS}$-$\mathrm{AS}$ problem posed by Brania and Yang.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The problem of nonparametric function fitting using the complete orthogonal system of trigonometric functions \(e_m\), \(m=0,\pm1, \pm2,\dots\), for the observation model \(y_j=d_jf(x_{jn})+\eta_j\), \(j=0, 1,\dots,n-1\), is considered, where \(f\colon[0,2\pi]\to\mathbb C\), \(\eta_j\) are uncorrelated random variables with zero mean value and finite variance, \(d_j\) are uncorrelated random variables with mean value \(d\neq0\) and finite variance, independent of \(\eta_j\), and the observation points \(x_{jn}\in[0,2\pi]\) are equidistant. Conditions for convergence of the integrated mean-square error \(E\| f-\hat f_{N(n)}\|^2_2\) and the pointwise mean-square error \(E(f(x)-\hat f_{N(n)}(x))^2\) of the estimator \(\hat f_{N(n)}(x)=\sum^{N(n)}_{m=-N(n)}\tilde c_me_m(x)/d\) for \(f\in BV[0,2\pi]\) and coefficients \(\tilde c_{-N(n)},\dots,\tilde c_{N(n)}\) obtained by the least squares method are studied.

editorial_contributions.text: We investigate optical bistability in intersubband transitions of an asymmetric semiconductor quantum well structure that has equidistant transitions between three subbands of the system and is placed in a unidirectional cavity. The system is simultaneously coupled by a fundamental field and its second harmonic. The second harmonic field acts as a control field and significantly influences the optical bistability. In addition, the two-color coherent control of optical bistability by the relative phase of the fundamental and the second harmonic fields is shown. The influence of the electronic cooperation parameter on the OB behavior is also discussed. This investigation may be used for optimizing and controlling the optical switching process in the SQW solid-state system, which is much more practical than that in the atomic system because of its flexible design and the controllable interference strength.

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(C\) be a class of metric spaces. A metric space \((X, d)\) is said to be \(C\)-injective if, for all \((Y, \rho)\), \((Z, \delta) \in C\) and every pair of isometric embeddings
\[
f \colon Y \to X \text{ and } \varphi \colon Y \to Z,
\]
there exists an isometric embedding \(F \colon Z \to X\) such that \(F \circ \varphi = f\). The author says that a set \(R\) is a range set if \(R \subseteq [0, \infty)\) and \(0 \in R\). An ultrametric space \((X, d)\) is called \(R\)-valued if \(d(x, y) \in R\) for all \(x\), \(y \in X\).

For a cardinal \(\kappa\) and for a range set \(R\), we denote by \(\mathcal{N}(R, \kappa)\) the class of all \(R\)-valued ultrametric spaces \((X, d)\), such that \(\operatorname{card}(X) < \kappa\).

The first main result of the paper is a characterization of \(\mathcal{N}(R, \kappa)\)-injective ultrametric spaces for finite \(\kappa \geqslant 2\). To formulate this result the author introduces the following concepts.

Let \(B(a, r)\) denote the closed ball in an ultrametric space \((X, d)\) such that \(a\) is the center of the ball \(B(a, r)\) and \(r\) is the radius of this ball.

Let \(\kappa \leqslant \omega_0\) and \(R\) be a range set. An ultrametric space \((X, d)\) is said to be \((R, \kappa)\)-haloed if for every \(a \in X\) and for every \(r \in R \setminus \{0\}\), there exists an \(r\)-equidistant subset \(A\) of \(B(a, r)\) such that \(\kappa \leqslant \operatorname{card}(A)\).

Let \(\kappa \leqslant \omega_0\) and \(R\) be a range set. An ultrametric space \((X, d)\) is \((R, \kappa)\)-avoidant if for every \(a \in X\), every \(r \in R \setminus \{0\}\), and for every subset \(A\) of \(B(a, r)\) with \(\operatorname{card}(A) < \kappa\), there exists \(p \in B(a, r)\) such that \(d(x, p) = r\) for all \(x \in A\).

\textbf{Theorem}. Let \(R\) be a range set. Let \((X, d)\) be an \(R\)-valued ultrametric space. Then, for every fixed integer \(n \geqslant 1\), the following statements are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}
\item [(A1)] The space \((X, d)\) is \((R, n)\)-haloed.
\item [(A2)] The space \((X, d)\) is \((R, n)\)-avoidant.
\item [(A3)] The space \((X, d)\) is \(\mathcal{N}(R, n+1)\)-injective.
\end{itemize}
The author also gives characterizations of the Urysohn universal ultrametric spaces and describes the properties of such spaces.
